source_metadata.exact_title: A corpus-specific clinical RAG system matches or outperforms newer frontier LLMs on HealthBench
source_metadata.source_type: arXiv preprint / benchmark comparison and clinical RAG evaluation report

atoms.canonical_statement: The study evaluated the India-specific VITA clinical RAG system against GPT-5.4, o4-mini, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 on English-language HealthBench questions.

VITA is described as a retrieval-augmented generation system purpose-built for context-specific clinical knowledge retrieval in India, using disease-specific guidelines, India-specific antimicrobial resistance data, national formulary constraints, and resource-limited care protocols.
The VITA architecture and retrieval corpus are proprietary in this paper and are described in a separate companion preprint rather than in the evaluated PDF.

The primary evaluation used 4,023 English-language HealthBench questions, reported as 80.5% of the 5,000-question benchmark and 94.7% of its English subset, with identical prompts, physician-written HealthBench rubrics, and GPT-4.1 as judge.

English-language questions were identified with langdetect; 225 excluded questions were described as non-English or misclassified by the language detector, and the analysis assumed their exclusion was non-differential with respect to model performance.

The 4,023 questions were processed in four sequential batches during iterative pipeline development; the paper states that prompts, judge, and rubrics were identical across batches and that results were pooled.

The paper reports that all 4,023 VITA responses, batch assignments, and rubric-scoring outputs are openly available on Figshare at DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.33216993, while HealthBench questions, rubrics, and judge scripts are available in OpenAI simple-evals.
VITA earned 51.9% of possible rubric points in the primary 4,023-question evaluation and was ranked 1.

atoms.canonical_statement: The paper reports that general-purpose LLMs scored higher than VITA on communication quality and instruction following in the primary evaluation.

A sensitivity analysis re-ran a random fixed-seed 500-question subset against GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Pro, Grok 4.3, and VITA, with DeepSeek-V4-Pro as an open-weight judge and non-thinking mode for all five systems.

The sensitivity analysis was designed, executed, and scored by co-authors who are reported to hold no equity, financial interest, or advisory relationship with VITA and to have had no role in VITA development or the primary evaluation.
The sensitivity analysis used 500 rather than all 4,023 questions because generation and grading of five systems across the full set exceeded the independent group's compute budget.
GPT-5.5 had a mean per-question score of 52.0% (95% CI 49.4–54.5) in the 500-question sensitivity analysis.

atoms.canonical_statement: The paper reports that the 500-question subset identifiers, all five systems' responses, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro scoring outputs from the sensitivity analysis are openly available on Figshare at DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.33224340.
The authors conclude that benchmark performance does not establish the mechanism of VITA's performance and hypothesize that corpus specificity is a meaningful design variable in clinical RAG.
On a HealthBench question about Nipah virus exposure from raw date palm sap in Bangladesh, VITA scored 51 of 67 possible rubric points versus 33 of 67 for GPT-5.4.

atoms.canonical_statement: The paper interprets grounding as the principal benefit of corpus specificity and communication polish as its cost.
The authors argue that clinical AI evaluation should be context-sensitive and continuous because static benchmarks cannot fully represent diverse practice settings or rapid model iteration.
The GPT-4.1 judge and physician-written HealthBench rubrics were developed primarily in Western clinical contexts and may systematically undervalue responses calibrated to LMIC settings.
The English-only primary evaluation did not test HealthBench non-English scenarios, so it does not establish whether VITA's multilingual corpus helps or harms performance in those settings.

Under the neutral judge with current-generation comparators, VITA's aggregate lead was no longer statistically distinguishable from the best frontier model, and the authors state that the top ranking should be read as parity rather than a clear first place.

The authors conclude that a purpose-built clinical AI system can match or outperform frontier general-purpose LLMs on HealthBench and that which system class performs better depends on the specialized system, clinical context, and standard of care used for evaluation.
The paper states that CRASH Lab AI has received support from Google.org and OpenAI.
The paper states that SA is a paid consultant to Social Alpha, which funded VITA development.
The paper states that CM is a co-founder of VITA.
The paper states that PR and VS are members of the iKITES technical team that developed VITA.
